KP14 Cover's Theorem

Level: undergraduate, year 3

Pattern Recognition | Chapter 4, §4.13

Slides: read and download

Learning objectives

  • Use Cover's formula to compute the number of linear dichotomies and the probability of separable for NNN points in general position in lll dimensions.
  • Explain the critical point N=2(l+1)N=2(l+1)N=2(l+1) and the phase transition, and predict the probability after lifting.
  • Explain that lifting raises separability but does not guarantee generalization.

KP14 Cover's Theorem

One-sentence summary: The higher the dimension, the more likely a set of points with random labels is still linearly separable, and there is a sharp critical point N=2(l+1)N=2(l+1)N=2(l+1); this is the quantitative licence for lifting, but it only guarantees that the training data can be separated, not that they generalize.

1. How many splits

Plain explanation: does lifting really help? First count into how many two-class splits one line can cut some points.

Dichotomy: one way of labeling NNN points with two classes; the ones a line (hyperplane) can realize are the linear dichotomies. For three points all 8 labelings are separable by a line; for four points at the corners of a square 14 of the 16 labelings are separable and the 2 that are not put the diagonal pairs together, [(A,D),(B,C)][(A,D),(B,C)][(A,D),(B,C)], which are XOR and its mirror XNOR (A top-left, B bottom-left, C top-right, D bottom-right; checked one by one by a program).

Figure lec05-kp14-dichotomy: the 16 labelings, green separable and red not.

2. The counting formula

General position: points in lll dimensions with no l+1l+1l+1 of them on one (l−1)(l-1)(l−1)-dimensional hyperplane (in two dimensions, no three on a line).

Formal definition (Cover's formula, source):

O(N,l)=2∑i=0l(N−1i). O(N,l)=2\sum_{i=0}^{l}\binom{N-1}{i}. O(N,l)=2i=0∑l​(iN−1​).

Example: N=4,l=2N=4,l=2N=4,l=2: 2(1+3+3)=142(1+3+3)=142(1+3+3)=14; N=3N=3N=3: 2(1+2+1)=8=232(1+2+1)=8=2^32(1+2+1)=8=23. For N≤l+1N\le l+1N≤l+1, O=2NO=2^NO=2N: all labelings are separable. For l=2l=2l=2 and N=1..8N=1..8N=1..8, O=2,4,8,14,22,32,44,58O=2,4,8,14,22,32,44,58O=2,4,8,14,22,32,44,58 while 2N=2,4,8,16,32,64,128,2562^N=2,4,8,16,32,64,128,2562N=2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256.

4. The phase transition

Phase transition: the turn of the probability from 1 down to 0 gets sharper as the dimension grows, like water freezing. With N=r(l+1)N=r(l+1)N=r(l+1), at r=2r=2r=2, i.e. N=2(l+1)N=2(l+1)N=2(l+1), O(2l+2,l)=22l+1O(2l+2,l)=2^{2l+1}O(2l+2,l)=22l+1, so the probability is exactly 1/21/21/2 (checked for l=1..7l=1..7l=1..7). PPP at r=1.5r=1.5r=1.5 and 2.52.52.5: 0.75,0.310.75,0.310.75,0.31 for l=1l=1l=1; 0.97,0.080.97,0.080.97,0.08 for l=19l=19l=19; 1.00,0.00071.00,0.00071.00,0.0007 for l=99l=99l=99.

5. A random test

Each run draws NNN two-dimensional Gaussian points with random ±1\pm1±1 labels and uses a linear program to decide whether a separating line exists, 1500 runs each: 0.865 at N=4N=4N=4 (formula 0.875) and 0.503 at N=6N=6N=6 (formula 0.500). With 1500 runs the standard error is about 0.01, so the gap is about one standard error (program, designed here).

Figure lec05-kp14-mc: formula against simulation.

6. The effect of lifting

With the same random points and labels, [x1,x2][x_1,x_2][x1​,x2​] is l=2l=2l=2; adding x12,x22,x1x2x_1^2,x_2^2,x_1x_2x12​,x22​,x1​x2​ makes l=5l=5l=5. The formula predicts N=6≤l+1=6N=6\le l+1=6N=6≤l+1=6, so P=1P=1P=1. The simulation (1500 runs) gives 0.494 for the original two dimensions and 1.000 for the quadratic features.

Figure lec05-kp14-lift: the separable fraction before and after lifting.

7. How many dimensions

For N>l+1N>l+1N>l+1 some labelings fail; once the data exceed twice the degrees of freedom (l+1l+1l+1 adjustable parameters), N>2(l+1)N>2(l+1)N>2(l+1), the probability of separable drops below half. For N=100N=100N=100: l=40l=40l=40 gives 0.0350.0350.035; 484848 gives 0.420.420.42; 494949 exactly 0.50.50.5; 565656 gives 0.920.920.92; 606060 gives 0.9870.9870.987; 686868 gives 0.99990.99990.9999. To separate random labels by lifting, the dimension must reach about half the number of samples or more.

Figure lec05-kp14-need: the probability for N=100N=100N=100 against the dimension lll.

8. Separable is not general

Common misconception: after lifting, if the training data can be separated then new data will be classified correctly. Experiment (designed here): 5 two-dimensional Gaussian points with random labels and a separating hyperplane in the quadratic features (5 dimensions) was found in all 300 runs with training all right; then 200 fresh points, also with random labels, were only 50.4% right on average, which is guessing. Lifting only guarantees that the training data can be separated; only data with a pattern can be learned, and generalization is a separate matter (Chapter 5).

Figure lec05-kp14-gen: accuracy on training and new points.
